processing: Single buds or a bud with an opening leaf, withered lightly, rolled heavily, fully oxidised and dried, with the rolling broken up before oxidation.
harvest_season: Picking generally starts before Qingming, using the youngest early spring buds.
appearance_dry: Fine, tight strands with sharp tips and plenty of visible golden hairs.
taste_profile: Sweet, with a sweet-mellow body and a lasting aroma; Ninghong tea is known for an apple-like note.

brewing.notes: Bud-heavy tea, so water well below boiling keeps it sweet. A gaiwan shows the golden tips well; do not rush the first couple of steeps with hot water.

vintage_note: Sold by spring harvest, mainly current-year, and priced by how early and how tippy the picking is. It is usually drunk within a year or two, though one storage study found honey and fruit notes grow with age as the floral side fades. Grades follow the provincial standard DB36/T 1943-2024.
description:
Ninghong Jinhao is the golden-tip top end of Ninghong, the old black tea of Xiushui in northwest Jiangxi. Ninghong itself is counted among China's earliest gongfu blacks; Jinhao is what you get when that tradition is made almost entirely from buds.

The leaf is a bud alone or a bud with one barely opened leaf, largely from the local Ningzhou group variety. Ninghong's own craft signature is a light wither, heavy rolling and full oxidation. Because so much of the tea is fine hair, the finished leaf looks golden rather than black.

The cup is a clear orange-red, sweet and mellow, with a lasting aroma; Ninghong's characteristic note is often described as apple. Being bud-based, it dislikes boiling water, so go cooler and keep steeps short and it stays sweet rather than sharp.

A Jiangxi provincial standard now sets out the grades: the best should be fine, sharp-tipped and visibly golden. Look for the harvest date and a Xiushui producer, and be wary of tea that is only dusted with gold-looking tips in a darker, coarser base.
history:
Ninghong's black tea craft is traced to the late Qianlong era of the Qing dynasty, grew in name through the early Daoguang years and peaked under Guangxu. From the mid-19th century it travelled overseas as a well-known export black tea. The technique is on China's national intangible heritage list.

Jinhao is the modern bud-grade expression of that tradition, and now has its own Jiangxi provincial standard, DB36/T 1943-2024. When it was first made as a separate product is less clearly documented.
